content: Healthcare providers must consult the Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) guidelines on antiretroviral (ARV) interactions when advising women living with HIV about the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptive methods. Women living with HIV who are on ARVs should discuss with their healthcare providers how specific ARVs may impact contraceptive efficacy, as recommendations vary depending on the stage of HIV progression. This highlights the importance of ensuring access to a comprehensive range of contraceptive options, informed decision-making, and supportive healthcare providers. Women living with HIV should feel empowered to explore their contraceptive options thoroughly. The updated third edition of the WHO’s Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use (SPR), published in 2016, provides detailed guidance on the safe and effective use of contraceptive methods once deemed medically appropriate. The SPR complements the MEC, which focuses on the safety of contraceptive methods in the context of specific health conditions and characteristics. According to the MEC, most contraceptive methods can be safely and effectively used by women with asymptomatic HIV infection or AIDS. Condoms remain a critical component of HIV prevention programs and are essential for comprehensive protection against sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and unintended pregnancies. Male and female condoms are particularly important for women living with HIV to protect themselves. To ensure safety and effectiveness, condoms must meet international standards and quality assurance procedures established by WHO, UNFPA, and ISO. They should also be made available free of charge or at affordable prices, as people in low-resource settings are more likely to use condoms when they are accessible at no cost or subsidized rates. Many young women, particularly those in long-term relationships or engaged in sex work, often lack the power to negotiate condom use due to resistance from male partners, who typically hold more power in these relationships. Suggesting condom use within a relationship may be perceived as a lack of trust or intimacy. Counseling by healthcare providers is essential to help women identify their fertility desires and provide information about the full range of contraceptive options if they wish to avoid pregnancy voluntarily. The WHO’s 2012 counseling tool for reproductive choices and family planning for people living with HIV guides providers through a structured process to assess, advise, agree, assist, and arrange care. Family planning counseling tailored to the needs and rights of women living with HIV is crucial for advancing their sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR). Ensuring high-quality care in contraceptive services is vital for achieving optimal health outcomes. Contraceptive programs must include elements such as a wide range of contraceptive options, evidence-based information on effectiveness and risks, trained healthcare workers, respect for informed choice and confidentiality, and integrated services at the same location. WHO tools, such as the Medical Eligibility Criteria Wheel for Contraceptive Use (2015 update) and the fifth edition of the MEC (2015), help healthcare providers and clients identify the best contraceptive options based on individual health status. The SPR (2016) provides additional guidance on safe contraceptive practices. It is essential that contraceptive services are free, voluntary, and non-coercive, particularly for key populations, including women in prisons, transgender women, female sex workers, and women who use drugs. Women living with HIV have reported being offered limited contraceptive options and, in some cases, being coerced into accepting long-term or permanent methods. Male condoms are both an enabler and a challenge for safe and pleasurable sexual experiences, but access to female condoms remains limited. Restricting contraceptive choices to methods requiring partner cooperation may increase the risk of unintended pregnancies, as many women face difficulties negotiating consistent condom use. Nearly 60% of women living with HIV surveyed had experienced an unplanned pregnancy, and only 40% had accessed family planning services. Many women, including adolescents and sex workers, lack adequate education and awareness about sexuality, pregnancy, and contraception. Gender dynamics significantly influence decision-making around contraception and family planning. WHO strongly recommends against routinely offering elective cesarean sections (C-sections) to women living with HIV unless medically indicated. The risks and benefits of different delivery modes, including vaginal delivery and elective or non-elective C-sections, should be discussed with women living with HIV. C-sections should only be performed for standard obstetric indications, as unnecessary C-sections can pose significant risks, particularly in settings with limited capacity to manage complications. Women living with HIV should be empowered to make informed decisions about delivery modes, and healthcare providers must avoid coercion or forced sterilization, which is never acceptable. In many high-HIV-burden settings, access to medically indicated C-sections is limited, especially in rural areas. When medically necessary, C-sections should be safe, accessible, and affordable. Elective C-sections may reduce infant HIV transmission but increase maternal and infant morbidity. The decision to perform a C-section must consider the risks and benefits for both mother and infant, taking into account the stage of HIV progression, antiretroviral therapy (ART) use, and the risks associated with surgical delivery compared to vaginal delivery. Women living with HIV often report being excluded from decision-making about their sexual and reproductive health, including delivery modes. Human rights principles must be embedded in all healthcare policies and practices, ensuring that coercion is never acceptable. Respectful, non-discriminatory care is essential to protect the rights and health of women living with HIV and their infants.
